summary:
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines criminalises consensual sex between men. Section 146 of the criminal code, the inherited buggery offence, carries up to 10 years' imprisonment; section 148, gross indecency, carries up to 5 years. Both provisions remain in force.

On 16 February 2024 the High Court dismissed a constitutional challenge and upheld the ban, holding that outlawing homosexual activity is lawful. The Eastern Caribbean rights alliance ECADE condemned the ruling on 19 February 2024, stating that LGBTQ+ Vincentians face greater vulnerability as a result. The Prime Minister has said any change would be an OECS-wide decision, because constitutional and legislative provisions are similar across member states.

Human Rights Watch's July 2023 report, a 58-page study titled 'They Can Harass Us Because of the Laws', documents bias-motivated violence and discrimination against LGBT people in daily life and calls for decriminalisation and for sexual-orientation and gender-identity non-discrimination legislation. No law addresses discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so LGBT people have no legal protection when they speak out.

In September 2018 three cross-dressing young men were physically attacked; Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves condemned the attacks, called the homophobia unacceptable and called for an open conversation on homosexuality. In April 2019 a cross-dressing teenager, Leswan Stewart, was the victim of a transphobic assault and was then charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman; the prosecutor withdrew the charge in May 2019 without giving a reason.

The country does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnership, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the rights given to married couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law has no route to recognition.

No organisation dedicated to LGBT people operates in the country and no helpline or help centre for LGBT youth exists, so dedicated support is absent. The sources do not cover healthcare, medication or HIV service provision beyond naming the Caribbean HIV/AIDS Alliance as the main contact point for men who have sex with men. Social infrastructure is thin, and LGBT life is largely invisible and stigmatised.

No visa, entry-screening or admission rule affecting LGBT travellers appears in the sources.
tangentialFactors:
In September 2011 an article by a same-sex couple in the local publication Vinci Kallaloo drew over 3,400 hits in under a day and more than 50 comments, several containing violent murderous threats.

A 53-year-old Vincentian resident of Chicago, Sean Macleish, publicly advocated to the Prime Minister for removal of the laws so he could return home with his partner, without effect.
localsOnly:
Men who have sex with men frequently marry women and live discreetly. No organisation dedicated to LGBT people operates in the country and no helpline or help centre for LGBT youth exists.

In 2011 three lecturers at the St. Vincent and the Grenadines Community College were targeted by the college's director in an orchestrated scheme accusing them of 'homosexual tendencies', allegedly to fire political opponents.

Two men left the country because of the law. Javin Johnson, 22, won asylum in the United Kingdom in 2017 after establishing he could not live as a gay man in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. In their 2019 affidavits two petitioners stated that the legislation had exiled them from the country because of its severely draconian and damaging effects.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust page documenting Eastern Caribbean constitutional challenges could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), so its account of the litigation is not available here.

No law governing gender markers on travel or identity documents is sourced, and no data on how often sections 146 and 148 are enforced, or on recent prosecutions, is available.

No trans-specific violence statistics with denominators are available; the documented incidents are individual cases.

No information on facilities law or practice, or on screening procedures at entry, is sourced.
